claim: 46.5% of Indians tested show vitamin D deficiency and an additional 26% have insufficient levels, meaning nearly three-quarters of Indians have suboptimal vitamin D status, per Metropolis Healthcare's nationwide study of 22 lakh test results (2019-2025).
stance_target: Vitamin D deficiency is a mass-market public health problem in India justifying widespread supplementation
scope_conditions: India; 22 lakh (2.2 million) test results; 2019 to January 2025
quoted_support: 46.5 percent of individuals tested showed deficient levels, while an additional 26 percent had insufficient vitamin D. This widespread inadequacy underscores a significant public health challenge in the country.

claim: South India has the highest vitamin D deficiency rate in India at 51.6%, with Kerala, Puducherry, and Tamil Nadu each exceeding 50%.
stance_target: Southern India is a high-priority region for vitamin D supplementation marketing
scope_conditions: India; regional breakdown from Metropolis Healthcare study; 2019-2025
quoted_support: South India recorded the highest deficiency rates at 51.6 percent. Notably, states like Kerala, Puducherry, and Tamil Nadu each reported levels exceeding the 50 percent mark.

claim: Indian teenagers (aged 13-18 years) have the highest vitamin D deficiency rate of any age group at 66.9%, pointing to a growing adolescent health concern.
stance_target: Younger demographics including teenagers are a key target market for vitamin D supplements
scope_conditions: India; age-stratified from Metropolis Healthcare study; 2019-2025
quoted_support: Teenagers, aged 13–18 years, registered the highest deficiency rate at 66.9 percent. This alarming statistic highlights a growing adolescent health concern.

claim: National vitamin D deficiency in India declined from approximately 51% (2019-20) to 43% (2023-24), showing gradual improvement but still critically high levels.
stance_target: Awareness and supplementation interventions are having modest positive effects in India
quoted_support: Deficiency levels declined from approximately 51 percent in 2019–20 to 43 percent in 2023–24. Despite this positive trajectory, medical professionals warn about continuous challenges.

claim: Traditional Indian vegetarian and lacto-vegetarian diets rarely include vitamin D-rich foods like fatty fish or fortified dairy, compounding deficiency risk from limited sun exposure.
stance_target: Dietary habits in India make supplementation especially necessary for vegetarians
quoted_support: Many traditional Indian diets often lack sufficient vitamin D-rich foods. This is especially true for vegetarian and lacto-vegetarian options, which rarely include fatty fish or fortified dairy products.
